$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(2-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2(2)-\frac{1}{2}({2}^{2})-(2(1)-\frac{1}{2}({1}^{2})) \\  & =4-2-2+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,J.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
F=ma=0.5\cdot (5-x)=(2.5-0.5x)\,N.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(2.5-0.5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{5}{2}x-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(2)-\frac{1}{4}({2}^{2})-(\frac{5}{2}(1)-\frac{1}{4}({1}^{2})) \\  & =5-1-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}

Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=2\,s.$" :question/worked-solution "The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 2t\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & ={t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0={0}^{2}+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\,s$ is

$$
v=v(2)={2}^{2}=4\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {4}^{2} \\  & =16\,J.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cb6dfeb2-3a92-53e8-a0f6-ee617bbb1e9c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{t+1}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\operatorname{ln}⁡|0+1|+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=3\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+1|=\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|3+1|=2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2} \\  & =8{ln}^{2}⁡2-2{ln}^{2}⁡2 \\  & =6{ln}^{2}⁡(2)\,J.\end{aligned}

Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=0\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$" :question/worked-solution "The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. $$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The displacement of the particle is given by $x(t)={t}^{2}+t+1,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by differentiating the displacement with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t+1) \\  & =2t+1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=0$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(0)=2(0)+1=1\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=2(2)+1=5\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {5}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{75}{2}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =36\,J.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-26a75307-ee16-5df7-9ca9-2990c5ceb006"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-26a75307-ee16-5df7-9ca9-2990c5ceb006" :answer-field/id #uuid "26a75307-ee16-5df7-9ca9-2990c5ceb006" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c4de12ba-3316-5e1b-ac4d-ff0026c7af55" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9085cdd3-9d32-5301-8cbf-ca557b3f00d6" "answer-fab72cab-a457-504c-bec5-6f9514a2cbb6" "answer-c8dba406-896d-56df-ba18-d38eb5a20778" "answer-c4de12ba-3316-5e1b-ac4d-ff0026c7af55" "answer-93b0a24f-9f97-5f8e-ae03-d64c89bef3e8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9085cdd3-9d32-5301-8cbf-ca557b3f00d6" :answer/id #uuid "9085cdd3-9d32-5301-8cbf-ca557b3f00d6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "20\,J" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fab72cab-a457-504c-bec5-6f9514a2cbb6" :answer/id #uuid "fab72cab-a457-504c-bec5-6f9514a2cbb6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "25\,J" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c8dba406-896d-56df-ba18-d38eb5a20778" :answer/id #uuid "c8dba406-896d-56df-ba18-d38eb5a20778" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "27\,J" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c4de12ba-3316-5e1b-ac4d-ff0026c7af55" :answer/id #uuid "c4de12ba-3316-5e1b-ac4d-ff0026c7af55" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "36\,J" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-93b0a24f-9f97-5f8e-ae03-d64c89bef3e8" :answer/id #uuid "93b0a24f-9f97-5f8e-ae03-d64c89bef3e8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "49\,J" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-34ad571d-a040-5724-a4dd-5d1ff6b4a0c6" :question/id #uuid "34ad571d-a040-5724-a4dd-5d1ff6b4a0c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-163674" :question/problem "A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$

$$

and final velocity, at $t=3$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(3)=3(3)^{2}=27\,m/s.
$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-163703" :question/problem "A particle $P$ of mass $\frac{1}{2}\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(3-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters, the particle is initially at $x=1,$ and the particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=4,$ find the particle's change in velocity in moving from $x=1$ to $x=4.$" :question/worked-solution "The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[3x+\frac{1}{x}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(12+\frac{1}{4})-(3+1) \\  & =\frac{33}{4}\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=4.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=1$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{33}{4} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {7}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{33}{4} & =\frac{49}{4}-\frac{1}{4}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{4}{v}_{0}^{2} & =4 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=1$ is $4\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=1$ to $x=4$ is

$$
{v}_{1}-{v}_{0}=7-4=3\,m/s.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a9005e61-607d-5045-aa66-20814a697f93"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id That is,

$$

$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3{x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}+x{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1+1-0 \\  & =2\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at $x=1.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=0$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}{m}_{1}{v}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 2 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {4}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 2 & =8-\frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =6 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =12 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=0$ is $2\sqrt{3}\,m/s.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-685ebe43-4362-5e9f-b513-b366e7e5ddc5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-685ebe43-4362-5e9f-b513-b366e7e5ddc5" :answer-field/id #uuid "685ebe43-4362-5e9f-b513-b366e7e5ddc5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-86e20970-7c3b-5405-aba7-818b64498280" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5af78eb7-b0ac-5fb4-8298-83843c06cabd" "answer-86e20970-7c3b-5405-aba7-818b64498280" "answer-c6037124-9ca8-59a2-a5ba-448ad5035b07" "answer-c6e877fb-7b90-52aa-a3a8-3a656bf7b8f5" "answer-7a400848-d283-509d-b2ce-69f7f8a4002f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5af78eb7-b0ac-5fb4-8298-83843c06cabd" :answer/id #uuid "5af78eb7-b0ac-5fb4-8298-83843c06cabd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}\,m/s" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-86e20970-7c3b-5405-aba7-818b64498280" :answer/id #uuid "86e20970-7c3b-5405-aba7-818b64498280" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}\,m/s" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c6037124-9ca8-59a2-a5ba-448ad5035b07" :answer/id #uuid "c6037124-9ca8-59a2-a5ba-448ad5035b07" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\,m/s" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c6e877fb-7b90-52aa-a3a8-3a656bf7b8f5" :answer/id #uuid "c6e877fb-7b90-52aa-a3a8-3a656bf7b8f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\sqrt{2}\,m/s" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7a400848-d283-509d-b2ce-69f7f8a4002f" :answer/id #uuid "7a400848-d283-509d-b2ce-69f7f8a4002f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\,m/s" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180764 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll discuss the concepts of **work** and **kinetic energy** and describe how these concepts are related. 

The **work done by the force** $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from the position $x=x_1$ to the position $x=x_2$ along the $x$-axis is defined as

$$
W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons ($\textrm{N}$) and meters ($\textrm{m}$), respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($\rm{J}$).

For example, suppose a particle $P$ is moving along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $4x^3\,\textrm{N},$ acting in the direction of increasing $x,$ as shown below. Distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters.

![](images/3f/3f0040d7a71563304cb954908988c82df1774a1197a5ce16c74a3b8ac65e04a0.png)

 

Let's calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

Substituting the given values into our formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =16-1 \\  & =15\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the work done by $F$ in moving $P$ from $x_1=1\,\textrm m$ to $x_2=2\,\textrm m$ equals $15\,\textrm J.$

We can use the concept of work in conjunction with Newton's second law. Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180766 :tutorial/content "The **work-energy principle** states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W = \Delta\, \text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
\Delta\, \text{KE} = \dfrac12 m v_1^2 - \dfrac12 m v_0^2
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, $v_0$ is its initial velocity, and $v_1$ is its final velocity." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179842 :activity/expected-seconds 1080.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(3x+1.5)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}({2}^{2}+2-({1}^{2}+1)) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(6-2) \\  & =6\,J.\end{aligned}

$$

Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=3\,s.$" :question/worked-solution "The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{t+1}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\operatorname{ln}⁡|0+1|+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=3\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+1|=\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|3+1|=2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2} \\  & =8{ln}^{2}⁡2-2{ln}^{2}⁡2 \\  & =6{ln}^{2}⁡(2)\,J.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d1a23531-d7b7-5e92-b4ab-f45652f32a5c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=3\,s.$" :question/worked-solution "The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =-\frac{1}{t+1}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=-\frac{1}{0+1}+C\,⟹\,C=1.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=1-\frac{1}{t+1}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=3\,s$ is

$$
v=v(3)=1-\frac{1}{3+1}=\frac{3}{4}\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=3$ is

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int (1+2t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =t+{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=0+{0}^{2}+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=t+{t}^{2}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\,s$ is

$$
v=v(2)=2+{2}^{2}=6\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot {6}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot 36 \\  & =27\,J.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d5e2fc07-70cb-5248-ae29-9ab2d781882c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d5e2fc07-70cb-5248-ae29-9ab2d781882c" :answer-field/id #uuid "d5e2fc07-70cb-5248-ae29-9ab2d781882c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e23afd90-794c-56ba-9d78-eb6940eb6376" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c924bbae-ceed-5733-99b9-207c3ea0be7d" "answer-6a368a44-5bac-522d-9eaa-44cf19404a5e" "answer-e23afd90-794c-56ba-9d78-eb6940eb6376" "answer-4ec6c244-5362-5ac9-9cb2-e52010f2e97e" "answer-562735b2-f2b9-5808-9e01-b4da0083cca1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c924bbae-ceed-5733-99b9-207c3ea0be7d" :answer/id #uuid "c924bbae-ceed-5733-99b9-207c3ea0be7d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "18\,J" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6a368a44-5bac-522d-9eaa-44cf19404a5e" :answer/id #uuid "6a368a44-5bac-522d-9eaa-44cf19404a5e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "24\,J" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e23afd90-794c-56ba-9d78-eb6940eb6376" :answer/id #uuid "e23afd90-794c-56ba-9d78-eb6940eb6376" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "27\,J" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4ec6c244-5362-5ac9-9cb2-e52010f2e97e" :answer/id #uuid "4ec6c244-5362-5ac9-9cb2-e52010f2e97e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32\,J" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-562735b2-f2b9-5808-9e01-b4da0083cca1" :answer/id #uuid "562735b2-f2b9-5808-9e01-b4da0083cca1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "36\,J" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180105 :question/problem "A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. $$

$$

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =16+16-0 \\  & =32\,J\end{aligned}
$$

$$

particle's change in velocity in moving from $x=1$ to $x=4.$" :question/worked-solution "The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[3x+\frac{1}{x}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(12+\frac{1}{4})-(3+1) \\  & =\frac{33}{4}\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=4.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=1$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{33}{4} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {7}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{33}{4} & =\frac{49}{4}-\frac{1}{4}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{4}{v}_{0}^{2} & =4 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=1$ is $4\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=1$ to $x=4$ is

$$

The **work done by the force** $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from the position $x=x_1$ to the position $x=x_2$ along the $x$-axis is defined as

$$
W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons ($\textrm{N}$) and meters ($\textrm{m}$), respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($\rm{J}$).

For example, suppose a particle $P$ is moving along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $4x^3\,\textrm{N},$ acting in the direction of increasing $x,$ as shown below. Distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters.

![](images/3f/3f0040d7a71563304cb954908988c82df1774a1197a5ce16c74a3b8ac65e04a0.png)

 

Let's calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

Substituting the given values into our formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =16-1 \\  & =15\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the work done by $F$ in moving $P$ from $x_1=1\,\textrm m$ to $x_2=2\,\textrm m$ equals $15\,\textrm J.$

We can use the concept of work in conjunction with Newton's second law. Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180766 :tutorial/content "The **work-energy principle** states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. $$

$$

$$

$$
v=v(1)=2({1}^{3/2})=2\,m/s.
$$

$$

Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=3\,s.$"] ["question-2dec6491-4f2e-5985-9f0d-5f140c0cfaf3" :question/worked-solution "The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{t+1}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\operatorname{ln}⁡|0+1|+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=3\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+1|=\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|3+1|=2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2} \\  & =8{ln}^{2}⁡2-2{ln}^{2}⁡2 \\  & =6{ln}^{2}⁡(2)\,J.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2dec6491-4f2e-5985-9f0d-5f140c0cfaf3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d1a23531-d7b7-5e92-b4ab-f45652f32a5c" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =16+16-0 \\  & =32\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=5\,m/s$ at $x=2.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=0$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 32 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {5}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 32 & =50-2{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 2{v}_{0}^{2} & =18 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =9 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=0$ is $3\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is

$$

["question-a80bea3f-8cb9-59ff-8c63-3325a8f0a338" :question/worked-solution "The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[3x+\frac{1}{x}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(12+\frac{1}{4})-(3+1) \\  & =\frac{33}{4}\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=4.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=1$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{33}{4} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {7}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{33}{4} & =\frac{49}{4}-\frac{1}{4}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{4}{v}_{0}^{2} & =4 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=1$ is $4\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=1$ to $x=4$ is

$$
{v}_{1}-{v}_{0}=7-4=3\,m/s.
$$"] ["question-a80bea3f-8cb9-59ff-8c63-3325a8f0a338" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-a9005e61-607d-5045-aa66-20814a697f93" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

\[

and final velocity, at [math]t=2[/math], is
\[

\]

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int (4t+1)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =2{t}^{2}+t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0) = 0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0 = 2(0^2) + 0 + C
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
C = 0.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {10}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =100-9 \\  & =91\,J.\end{aligned}

The displacement of the particle is given by $(t^2-2t+3)\,\rm{m},$ where $t \geq 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,\rm{s}$ and $t=3\,\rm{s}.$" :question/worked-solution "The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W
= 
\Delta\, \text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
\Delta\, \text{KE} = \dfrac12 m v_1^2 - \dfrac12 m v_0^2
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, $v_0$ is its initial velocity, and $v_1$ is its final velocity.

The displacement of the particle is given by $x(t)=t^2-2t+3,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by differentiating the displacement with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t+3) \\  & =2t-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1$, is

$$
v_0 = v(1) =  2(1) -2 = 0\,\rm{m/s},
$$

and its final velocity, at $t=3$, is

$$
v_1 = v(3) = 2(3) -2= 4\,\rm{m/s}.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot (4)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{2} \\  & =8-0 \\  & =8\,J.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180103 :question/id #uuid "c92a85dc-fea5-582a-a4d0-c749606f94b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-163601"} {:db/id 17592186180105 :question/id #uuid "93920b26-fb04-52d5-8d58-1e17f6af55c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-163663" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179779 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "94904fa2-bf02-5486-950c-979a4d12998e" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Work-Energy Principle To Find the Work Done by a Force"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9df22e30-1b2f-5c18-a7fe-a7be5f1b8885" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "36J" :db/id 17592186178300} {:answer/id #uuid "bdb34d99-42e0-54b9-9c21-280b28a37857" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "20J" :db/id 17592186178301} {:answer/id #uuid "cb5b140a-60cf-5cf2-9e20-1f0817120212" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "25J" :db/id 17592186178302} {:answer/id #uuid "ce23d63c-bb7d-542f-97c1-7ddc64a45394" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "49J" :db/id 17592186178303} {:answer/id #uuid "0d225512-d29c-55c9-81ee-3ca1ed789e2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "27J" :db/id 17592186178304}] :answer-field/id #uuid "a3ef2f1d-303e-5a18-8c46-581a2ecef6e1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186178299}] :question/problem "A particle $P$ of mass $3kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. $$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The particle's velocity is given by $v(t)=t+1,$ where $t$ is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(2)=2+1=3\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=4$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(4)=4+1=5\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot (5)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot (3)^{2} \\  & =\frac{25}{2}-\frac{9}{2} \\  & =8\,J.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186389442 :question/id #uuid "f249579b-a99f-5b51-b0c7-e7f72d9a4512" :question/math-academy-id "q-163678"} {:db/id 17592186179780 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id $$
W

$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
\Delta\, \text{KE} = \dfrac12 m v_1^2 - \dfrac12 m v_0^2
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, $v_0$ is its initial velocity, and $v_1$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=2$ to $x=4{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{4}(x+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+3x]}_{2}^{4} \\  & =(8+12)-(2+6) \\  & =12\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ at $x=2.$ So, we can find the velocity $v_1$ at $x=4$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 12 & ={v}_{1}^{2}-4 \\ {v}_{1}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration.

"64ed08fd-258d-5456-ab85-4c3d693a62d2" :topic/math-academy-id 3687} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180573 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180764 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll discuss the concepts of **work** and **kinetic energy** and describe how these concepts are related. 

The **work done by the force** $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from the position $x=x_1$ to the position $x=x_2$ along the $x$-axis is defined as

$$
W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons ($\textrm{N}$) and meters ($\textrm{m}$), respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($\rm{J}$).

For example, suppose a particle $P$ is moving along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $4x^3\,\textrm{N},$ acting in the direction of increasing $x,$ as shown below. Distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters.

![](images/3f/3f0040d7a71563304cb954908988c82df1774a1197a5ce16c74a3b8ac65e04a0.png)

Let's calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

Substituting the given values into our formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =16-1 \\  & =15\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the work done by $F$ in moving $P$ from $x_1=1\,\textrm m$ to $x_2=2\,\textrm m$ equals $15\,\textrm J.$

We can use the concept of work in conjunction with Newton's second law. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "33cf6fa3-5f8d-579b-990b-ddeb9d1e3b8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7799 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "fa2ce148-bfaa-55f3-a775-56631c5bd980" 17592186284408} {:db/id 17592186284409} {:db/id 17592186284410} {:db/id 17592186284411} {:db/id 17592186389456}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Work-Energy Principle to Find a Particle's Velocity"} :step/id #uuid "b02a7662-acf4-57da-98d7-bae7093076f2" :step/math-academy-id 45126} {:db/id 17592186180578 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180765 :tutorial/content "The **kinetic energy** of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12mv^2.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms ($\rm{kg}$) and meters per second ($\rm{m/s}$), respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($\rm{J}$). 

For example, suppose a particle $P$ of mass $5\,\rm{kg}$ is moving along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of $3t^2\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ where $t \geq 0$ is the time in seconds. Let's calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=2\,\rm{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & ={t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0 = 0^3 + C
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
C = 0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = t^3.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\,\rm{s}$ is

$$
v=v(2) = 2^3 = 8\,\rm{m/s}.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5\cdot {8}^{2} \\  & =160\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- Kinetic energy is a *scalar* quantity.

- You probably noticed that kinetic energy and work have the same units. This is not a coincidence! We'll learn more about that shortly.

- In practical applications, it's often more important to calculate a *change* in the kinetic energy of a particle between two points in time. 

The **change in kinetic energy** of a particle with mass $m,$ **initial velocity** $v_0,$ and **final velocity** $v_1$ is given by

$$
\Delta \, \text{KE} = \dfrac12mv_1^2 - \dfrac12mv_0^2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "42f83ae3-3805-546b-a5bf-264b8b56d6ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7811 :tutorial/title "Kinetic Energy"} :step/id #uuid "3bec1351-7ee4-5f29-8760-5dd679edda2e" :step/math-academy-id 45179 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180575}} {:db/id 17592186180579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180766 :tutorial/content "The **work-energy principle** states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W = \Delta\, \text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
\Delta\, \text{KE} = \dfrac12 m v_1^2 - \dfrac12 m v_0^2
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, $v_0$ is its initial velocity, and $v_1$ is its final velocity.

For example, let a particle [math]P[/math] of mass [math]5\,\rm{kg}[/math] is moving along the [math]x[/math]-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is [math]4t\,\rm{m/s},[/math] where [math]t \geq 0[/math] is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times [math]t=1\,\rm{s}[/math] and [math]t=2\,\rm{s}.[/math]

The particle's velocity is given by [math]v(t)=4t,[/math] where [math]t[/math] is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at [math]t=1[/math], is
\[
v_0 = v(1) = 4(1) = 4\,\rm{m/s},
\]
and final velocity, at [math]t=2[/math], is
\[
v_1 = v(2) = 4(2) = 8\,\rm{m/s}.
\]

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

\begin{align*}
W
&= \Delta\, \text{KE} \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac12 \cdot 5 \cdot (8)^2 - \dfrac12 \cdot 5 \cdot (4)^2 \\[5pt]
&= 160 - 40 \\[5pt]
&= 120\,\rm{J}.
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "e00f462b-c087-5c42-afc7-bfeffad5906b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7812 :tutorial/title "The Work-Energy Principle"} :step/id #uuid "4d3d3f00-8ddb-5882-984a-2f48d2b19da6" :step/math-academy-id 45180 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180576}}] :activity/title "The Work-Energy Principle" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179842} {:db/id 17592186180573 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180764 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll discuss the concepts of **work** and **kinetic energy** and describe how these concepts are related.

For example, suppose a particle $P$ is moving along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $4x^3\,\textrm{N},$ acting in the direction of increasing $x,$ as shown below. Distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters.

![](images/3f/3f0040d7a71563304cb954908988c82df1774a1197a5ce16c74a3b8ac65e04a0.png)

Let's calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

Substituting the given values into our formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =16-1 \\  & =15\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the work done by $F$ in moving $P$ from $x_1=1\,\textrm m$ to $x_2=2\,\textrm m$ equals $15\,\textrm J.$

We can use the concept of work in conjunction with Newton's second law. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "33cf6fa3-5f8d-579b-990b-ddeb9d1e3b8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7799 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "fa2ce148-bfaa-55f3-a775-56631c5bd980" :step/math-academy-id 45122 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180574}} {:db/id 17592186180764 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll discuss the concepts of **work** and **kinetic energy** and describe how these concepts are related. 

The **work done by the force** $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from the position $x=x_1$ to the position $x=x_2$ along the $x$-axis is defined as

$$
W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons ($\textrm{N}$) and meters ($\textrm{m}$), respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($\rm{J}$).

For example, suppose a particle $P$ is moving along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $4x^3\,\textrm{N},$ acting in the direction of increasing $x,$ as shown below. Distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters.

![](images/3f/3f0040d7a71563304cb954908988c82df1774a1197a5ce16c74a3b8ac65e04a0.png)

$$

Therefore, the work done by $F$ in moving $P$ from $x_1=1\,\textrm m$ to $x_2=2\,\textrm m$ equals $15\,\textrm J.$

We can use the concept of work in conjunction with Newton's second law. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "33cf6fa3-5f8d-579b-990b-ddeb9d1e3b8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7799 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186180574 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179777 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179438 :question/id #uuid "622bd0ff-d08a-5504-8b38-8bc388bfcbf5" :question/math-academy-id "e-12525"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9696b3f4-42c8-5796-be3a-6c59c9600c95" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049423} {:db/id 17592186050723}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180099} {:db/id 17592186180100} {:db/id 17592186284403} {:db/id 17592186284405} {:db/id 17592186284407} {:db/id 17592186389449}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Work Done by a Force"} :step/id #uuid "cb90c47f-c22d-5b7f-a72a-cfc50bb4fdcd" :step/math-academy-id 45123 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180578}} {:db/id 17592186180578 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180765 :tutorial/content "The **kinetic energy** of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12mv^2.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms ($\rm{kg}$) and meters per second ($\rm{m/s}$), respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($\rm{J}$). 

For example, suppose a particle $P$ of mass $5\,\rm{kg}$ is moving along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of $3t^2\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ where $t \geq 0$ is the time in seconds. Let's calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=2\,\rm{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & ={t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0 = 0^3 + C
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
C = 0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = t^3.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\,\rm{s}$ is

$$
v=v(2) = 2^3 = 8\,\rm{m/s}.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5\cdot {8}^{2} \\  & =160\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- Kinetic energy is a *scalar* quantity.

- You probably noticed that kinetic energy and work have the same units. This is not a coincidence! We'll learn more about that shortly.

- In practical applications, it's often more important to calculate a *change* in the kinetic energy of a particle between two points in time. 

The **change in kinetic energy** of a particle with mass $m,$ **initial velocity** $v_0,$ and **final velocity** $v_1$ is given by

$$
\Delta \, \text{KE} = \dfrac12mv_1^2 - \dfrac12mv_0^2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "42f83ae3-3805-546b-a5bf-264b8b56d6ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7811 :tutorial/title "Kinetic Energy"} :step/id #uuid "3bec1351-7ee4-5f29-8760-5dd679edda2e" :step/math-academy-id 45179 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180575}} {:db/id 17592186180575 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179778 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179439 :question/id #uuid "4e428ee4-0017-5e83-887c-26e723b4af08" :question/math-academy-id "e-12526"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ec390427-7510-57ea-aedf-a930284f93b5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049947}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180101} {:db/id 17592186180102} {:db/id 17592186284412} {:db/id 17592186284413} {:db/id 17592186284414} {:db/id 17592186389463} {:db/id 17592186389470}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Kinetic Energy of a Particle"} :step/id #uuid "54dddd69-accb-5eb8-beac-e9f9dbc87bf7" :step/math-academy-id 45124 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180579}} {:db/id 17592186180579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180766 :tutorial/content "The **work-energy principle** states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W = \Delta\, \text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
\Delta\, \text{KE} = \dfrac12 m v_1^2 - \dfrac12 m v_0^2
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, $v_0$ is its initial velocity, and $v_1$ is its final velocity.

For example, let a particle [math]P[/math] of mass [math]5\,\rm{kg}[/math] is moving along the [math]x[/math]-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is [math]4t\,\rm{m/s},[/math] where [math]t \geq 0[/math] is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times [math]t=1\,\rm{s}[/math] and [math]t=2\,\rm{s}.[/math]

The particle's velocity is given by [math]v(t)=4t,[/math] where [math]t[/math] is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at [math]t=1[/math], is
\[
v_0 = v(1) = 4(1) = 4\,\rm{m/s},
\]
and final velocity, at [math]t=2[/math], is
\[
v_1 = v(2) = 4(2) = 8\,\rm{m/s}.
\]

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

\begin{align*}
W
&= \Delta\, \text{KE} \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac12 \cdot 5 \cdot (8)^2 - \dfrac12 \cdot 5 \cdot (4)^2 \\[5pt]
&= 160 - 40 \\[5pt]
&= 120\,\rm{J}.
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "e00f462b-c087-5c42-afc7-bfeffad5906b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7812 :tutorial/title "The Work-Energy Principle"} :step/id #uuid "4d3d3f00-8ddb-5882-984a-2f48d2b19da6" :step/math-academy-id 45180 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180576}} {:db/id 17592186180576 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179779 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179440 :question/id #uuid "39eab788-1a8d-51af-b535-594cacc8ec2e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12527"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "94904fa2-bf02-5486-950c-979a4d12998e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180103} {:db/id 17592186180105} {:db/id 17592186284400} {:db/id 17592186284401} {:db/id 17592186284402} {:db/id 17592186376131} {:db/id 17592186389428} {:db/id 17592186389435} {:db/id 17592186389442}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Work-Energy Principle To Find the Work Done by a Force"} :step/id #uuid "496c1449-0914-5643-b8b4-95ec09fb5867" :step/math-academy-id 45125 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180577}} {:db/id 17592186180577 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179780 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179441 :question/id #uuid "8f79d7e9-377f-5012-a762-279839fc806a" :question/math-academy-id "e-12528"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "793154ca-29f0-5552-97cd-57acbc915966" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048187}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180106} {:db/id 17592186180107} {:db/id 17592186284404} {:db/id 17592186284406} {:db/id 17592186284408} {:db/id 17592186284409} {:db/id 17592186284410} {:db/id 17592186284411} {:db/id 17592186389456}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Work-Energy Principle to Find a Particle's Velocity"} :step/id #uuid "b02a7662-acf4-57da-98d7-bae7093076f2" :step/math-academy-id 45126} {:db/id 17592186180765 :tutorial/content "The **kinetic energy** of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

[17592186046660 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.
The course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in
